questions.prompt: For a perfect winter soup, put the onions and tomatoes in water and let them ___ for an hour.
questions.note: Simmer means to cook a liquid slowly, just below boiling — exactly what a soup does for an hour.
why: Sprinkle means to drop small pieces of something (salt, herbs) over a surface. You sprinkle herbs on top at the end; you can’t leave vegetables to “sprinkle” for an hour.
Blend means to mix things until they are smooth. It takes a minute in a blender and comes after the cooking, not instead of it.
Spread means to cover a surface with a soft substance, like butter on bread. It has nothing to do with cooking in water.

questions.prompt: Let’s eat at home tonight — it’s ___ cheaper than going to a restaurant.
questions.note: Miles + comparative is a casual way to say “much”: miles cheaper, miles better. In formal writing, use much or significantly.
why: Very goes with ordinary adjectives (very cheap), but never with comparatives. Very cheaper is incorrect.
Much more cheaper is a double comparative: cheaper already contains the idea of “more”. Say much cheaper.
Many goes with plural nouns (many restaurants), not with adjectives.

questions.prompt: Someone made a rude comment about my shirt, but I just ___ and forgot about it in five seconds.
questions.note: Shrug something off = treat it as unimportant and not let it worry you. With a pronoun, the object goes in the middle: shrug it off.
why: The verb is right, but the word order is wrong. With a pronoun (it, them, him), a separable phrasal verb must be split: shrug it off, never shrug off it.
Shrug out is not a phrasal verb with this meaning. The particle that means “getting rid of something” here is off.
Shrug down does not exist in English. The correct particle is off.

questions.prompt: The organisers ___ the food, so everyone at the party stayed hungry.
questions.note: Skimp on something = use too little of it to save money, so the quality suffers.
why: Splash out on means to spend a lot of money on something generously — the opposite situation. If they had splashed out on the food, nobody would be hungry.
Skim through means to read something quickly (skim through a report). It looks similar but is about reading, not saving money.
Right verb, wrong preposition. Skimp combines with on: skimp on food, skimp on quality.

questions.prompt: Heavy rain ruined the outdoor festival, but the team didn’t complain. They ___ and kept working.
options: knocked it out of the park
questions.note: Take it on the chin = accept a failure or a bad situation bravely, without complaining.
why: Knock it out of the park means to do something extremely well, better than expected. Here the festival was ruined — it is a story about bad luck, not success.
Hold the line means to stay firm when people push you to change something (hold the line on prices). Nobody is pressuring the team here; the point is accepting misfortune bravely.

Jump the gun means to do something too early, before the right moment — like a runner who starts before the starting pistol. Nothing here happened too early; the point is accepting bad luck without complaining.

questions.prompt: The concert was cancelled because of a hurricane. Under the contract, nobody pays a penalty, because a hurricane counts as an ___.
questions.note: Act of God is a legal term for a natural event (a flood, earthquake or hurricane) that no person can control or prevent.
why: An act of faith is an action that shows trust or belief, e.g. lending money to a stranger. It is not a natural disaster.
Act of war is a real legal term too, but it describes a hostile action by a country or army — a human decision, not the weather.
A godsend is something unexpected and very welcome. A hurricane that cancels a concert is the opposite.

questions.prompt: I don’t have Martin’s phone number. ___ anyone else in the office.
questions.note: Nor + helping verb + subject = “and also not”: Nor does anyone else. The helping verb comes first, and there is no not.
why: Nor is already negative. Adding doesn’t creates a double negative. Say Nor does…
Neither can start this kind of sentence, but it also needs a helping verb before the subject: Neither does anyone else. Without does, the sentence has no verb.
Also is not used to add a negative idea. Use nor/neither at the start, or either at the end: Nobody else has it either.

questions.prompt: She ___ her listening skills by watching one episode a day without subtitles.
questions.note: Hone /həʊn/ = make a skill better and better through practice. It was once the name of a stone used to sharpen knives: hone your skills, hone your craft.
why: Home (as in home in on) means to move or aim directly towards a target. It looks and sounds similar, but it needs in on and has a different meaning.
Sharp is an adjective, not a verb. The verb is sharpen — and sharpens her listening skills would be correct.
Whet also means “to sharpen a blade”, but figuratively it collocates with appetite or interest (whet your appetite), not with skills.

options: Seldom does he answers the phone
Seldom does he answer the phone
questions.note: After seldom / rarely / never at the start of a sentence, use question word order: helping verb + subject. With no helping verb, add do/does/did and keep the main verb in its base form.
why: This is normal statement word order. When seldom opens the sentence, inversion is required: Seldom does he… (Normal order is fine only if seldom moves inside: He seldom answers…)
The inversion is correct, but after does the main verb must be in the base form: does he answer, not does he answers.
In modern English only helping verbs move in front of the subject. Main verbs like answer do not invert — use do/does/did.

questions.prompt: I could hear only one speaker because the three talks were ___ — they all started at 2 p.m. in different rooms.
questions.note: Concurrent = happening at the same time. Concurrent sessions run in parallel, so you have to choose one.
why: Consecutive means one after another, without a break. If the talks were consecutive, you could attend all three.
Subsequent means “coming after something else” (subsequent events). It describes order in time, not things happening together.
Successive is a near synonym of consecutive: following one after another. It contradicts “they all started at 2 p.m.”

questions.prompt: Charging ten dollars for a small bottle of water is an ___ example of overpricing.
questions.note: Egregious /ɪˈɡriːdʒəs/ = very bad and easy for everyone to see. From Latin ex grege “out of the flock”: once a compliment, now it means standing out for being terrible. Typical collocations: egregious mistake, error, example.
why: Gregarious shares the same Latin root (grex, “flock”), but it means sociable, fond of company. It describes people, not prices.
Exemplary means excellent, a model for others — strongly positive. Ironically, that is close to what egregious meant centuries ago, but not today.
Egalitarian means believing that all people are equal. It looks similar at the start, but the meaning is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Investors panicked when a “safe” money market fund broke the buck. What does that mean?
options: The fund lost money on a single million-dollar trade.
The fund offered less bang for the buck than its competitors.
The fund stopped paying investors in cash.
The value of one share of the fund fell below one dollar.
questions.note: A money market fund aims to keep each share worth exactly $1. Breaking the buck means the value drops below that dollar — a rare and alarming event.
why: Traders do use a buck for one million dollars, but break the buck is a fixed phrase about a share value going under $1, not about one trade.
Bang for the buck means value for money. A fund with poor value would simply be a bad choice; investors would not panic about a collapse.
The phrase is not about how payments are made. It refers to the price of a share falling below the one-dollar mark.
